document.title: Comments of Hans Royal re the Interim Resource Adequacy Service proposed by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C
document.group: PJM Large Load definition, Registry and Interim Resource Adequacy Service

pages.text:
Comments of Hans Royal, Docket No. ER26-3515-000, page 1 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.
Docket No. ER26-3515-000
COMMENTS OF HANS ROYAL 
September 3, 2026 
1. Introduction and Interest of the Commenter 
I am an energy professional and researcher, and spent nearly two decades advising large electricity 
buyers on electricity procurement before turning to this research full time. I developed the 
Compute Heat Rate (CHR) framework to answer a practical question: how high can the price of 
electricity rise before AI data center workloads are no longer profitable? CHR expresses that 
threshold in dollars per megawatt-hour and reports it by workload type. I published the framework 
on SSRN in February 2026 (Royal, 2026, doi 10.2139/ssrn.6322318), and I update the underlying 
index quarterly at computeheatrate.com. PJM discussed CHR at pages 49 through 50 of its May 6, 
2026 white paper, Powering Reliability Through Market Design, in connection with demand-side 
price tolerance. 
I am filing these comments on my own behalf as an independent researcher. I publish the index 
and provide advisory work drawing on this research; I have no client with an interest in this 
proceeding, and I represent no load, supplier, or other market participant, nor am I asking the 
Commission to adopt CHR, or any other single metric, as a tariff standard. Instead, my point is 
narrower: PJM is proposing a framework under which large loads are identified and, through 
Transmission Owners and Electric Distributors, reduced and compensated during capacity 
shortages. Two facilities can look the same on an interconnection diagram and have radically 
different economic responses to interruption, so my recommendation is that the design leave room 
for that fact. 
2. Summary of Position 
PJM needs an interim answer to a real resource adequacy problem, and this filing is a reasonable 
one. I support approval of the Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS), the Large Load 
Registry, and the Bring Your Own New Capacity (BYONC) provisions. The July 27 Board 
framework followed a substantial stakeholder process and places the reliability obligation where 
it belongs: on new load that enters without bringing new supply, not on customers already served 
by the system. 
There is one issue the Commission should keep in view as it evaluates the filing and the work that 
will follow it, which is that large loads are not economically interchangeable. This shows up in 
three ways:

Comments of Hans Royal, Docket No. ER26-3515-000, page 2 
First, the cost of interrupting one large load can differ from the cost of interrupting another by well 
over an order of magnitude. The Q3 2026 CHR index puts the operating electricity threshold for 
internal, self-hosted AI inference at about $1,200 per MWh and the threshold for frontier inference 
at about $18,400 per MWh. The consumption-weighted figure is about $9,100 per MWh. A pro 
rata zonal allocation and one compensation rate wouldn’t adequately reflect the real economics.  
Second, the filing itself provides evidence of this economic spread. A load that arranges new 
capacity under the BYONC rules or installs enough backup generation to take its load off the 
system is paying for firmness. Another load may accept IRAS exposure and the accompanying 
credit. Those are different choices about the value of uninterrupted service. BYONC and the 
backup-generation provisions will begin sorting loads on that basis even though the tariff does not 
describe the process in those terms. 
Third, the Registry can capture what PJM learns from those choices. I am not proposing a new 
mandate for the interim phase. I am asking the Commission to encourage PJM to keep the Registry 
and IRAS flexible enough to support voluntary reduction preferences and, where states and 
Electric Distributors choose to use them, economically informed reduction priorities later. 
3. Background: What the Compute Heat Rate Measures 
CHR starts with the revenue earned by an AI workload and the energy needed to deliver the 
service. From published inputs and disclosed assumptions, it estimates the electricity price the 
workload can absorb before continued operation ceases to make economic sense. 
The index reports two related values. Long-run CHR asks whether it still makes sense to build and 
operate new capacity for the workload. Dispatch CHR, or CHR-D, asks a different question: after 
the facility has been built and its capital cost is sunk, at what hourly electricity price would a 
rational operator stop running? CHR-D is the more relevant value here because curtailment is an 
operating decision. 
The Q3 2026 index was published September 1. It reports a blended long-run CHR of 
approximately $5,630 per MWh and a blended CHR-D of approximately $9,070 per MWh. Those 
figures are about 113 and 181 times a conventional gas-fired reference price of $50 per MWh. The 
long-run CHR declined by nearly 30 percent from Q2, reflecting both market developments, 
including falling token prices and the commoditization of inference, and methodology updates 
disclosed with the release. That movement is important: the index tracks the market rather than 
fixing a number. It did not, however, change the basic result. For the commercial workloads that 
account for most deployed compute, the rational curtailment threshold remains far above any price 
PJM's energy market is permitted to produce. 
Those numbers require two qualifications. First, neither CHR nor CHR-D says whether a facility 
can physically reduce load in ten minutes, or by how much. That depends on the operator, the 
facility, and PJM's operating rules. Second, CHR is not a price forecast. It is an economic ceiling: 
a measure of economic tolerance, not a prediction of what power will cost.

Comments of Hans Royal, Docket No. ER26-3515-000, page 3 
4. Observations on the Proposal 
References below to the 'Board framework' are to PJM's CIFP Framework for Service During 
Periods of Insufficient Resource Adequacy (July 27, 2026), which the August 13, 2026 filing 
implements. Where the filed tariff language differs from that framework, the filed language 
controls. 
4.1 Curtailment economics are heterogeneous, and the spread is large 
The label "AI data center" hides a very wide range of economics. In the Q3 2026 index, CHR-D 
runs from approximately $1,227 per MWh for internal and self-hosted inference to approximately 
$18,378 per MWh for frontier inference, a spread of roughly fifteen times. At the low end, a 
compensated interruption may be a sensible bargain. At the high end, the lost workload value 
during the same hour can exceed the credit many times over. 
Electric Distributors would compensate compliant IRAS reductions at a single flat hourly rate set 
by PJM and tied to the rate already used for pre-emergency demand response (Board framework, 
Credits, item 6). Measured against CHR-D, that credit is likely to cover much of what some 
workloads lose and a small fraction of what others lose. 
4.2 What uniform treatment leaves on the table 
If PJM needs a given number of megawatts during an emergency, it can obtain those megawatts 
from loads with very different interruption costs. The framework allocates reductions across 
affected zones pro rata and leaves customer-specific implementation to Transmission Owners and 
Electric Distributors in coordination with states and affected customers, with no economic 
criterion. That order could cut a workload that would pay almost anything to continue operating 
while leaving another workload online that would have reduced voluntarily at a much lower price. 
Reliability sees the same megawatts either way; customers do not bear the same cost. Over time, 
PJM could reduce that cost by allowing loads to volunteer for earlier reduction or by permitting 
states and Electric Distributors to use economic exposure when setting reduction order. 
The single credit rate creates the same mismatch. The credit is below the operating value of most 
deployed compute as measured by CHR-D. I do not view that as a flaw in the proposed rate. Fully 
compensating frontier inference would impose an unreasonable cost on other customers, and the 
Board reasonably concluded that an IRAS reduction happens earlier and under less severe 
conditions than a full emergency. But the credit should not be mistaken for the value of the 
curtailed activity. A high-CHR-D load has little economic reason to rely on it and every reason to 
seek firmness through BYONC or on-site generation. A lower-CHR-D load may find the credit 
meaningful and may be willing to reduce first. 
4.3 The proposal already sorts loads by willingness to pay for firmness 
BYONC and the Registry's backup-generation field (Registration Content, item 10) will give PJM 
a rough but useful signal about the value that individual loads place on firmness. A customer that 
arranges BYONC backed by a resource subject to the proposal's maintenance and price-taker

Comments of Hans Royal, Docket No. ER26-3515-000, page 4 
requirements, or installs backup generation sufficient to remove its load from the system, has made 
an expensive choice not to be interrupted. 
This is why the economic spread is not merely theoretical. Once implementation begins, the 
Registry is expected to show some large loads arriving with BYONC or backup generation and 
others arriving without either. The proposal will produce economic differentiation through those 
customer choices. It simply does not yet use the resulting information when reductions are 
assigned. 
4.4 The Registry as a foundation 
The Board describes the Registry as providing "the critical data transparency needed to establish 
load reduction priorities for retail customers." It also commits PJM to publish aggregate 
information where confidentiality permits. I agree with both decisions. The Registry can also hold, 
on a voluntary basis, the information that states and Electric Distributors would need to set 
reduction order more intelligently when they "coordinate with the individual customers that will 
be subject to Interim Resource Adequacy Service" (Participation Details, item 9). 
PJM does not need to collect detailed economic data in this proceeding. It should, however, avoid 
designing a schema that forecloses the option. A voluntary field stating a customer's reduction 
preference, or noting planned participation in Price Responsive Demand or a state economic-
priority program, would be enough to preserve a path forward. Adding that capacity now is easier 
than rebuilding the Registry after it is populated. 
5. Recommendations 
I ask the Commission to take four steps: 
(a) Approve IRAS, the Large Load Registry, and BYONC as interim measures on PJM's 
requested schedule. 
(b) Recognize in its order that pro rata allocation and a uniform credit are interim 
simplifications. The Commission should encourage PJM and its stakeholders to examine 
economically differentiated participation and reduction order in the follow-on process. 
That work could use Price Responsive Demand, state and Electric Distributor programs 
informed by Registry data, voluntary self-designation, or a combination of those 
approaches. 
(c) Encourage PJM to include voluntary Registry fields that can support that work and to 
publish enough aggregate detail for independent analysis of how large loads are actually 
entering the system. 
(d) Encourage the use of transparent, published, independently verifiable economic 
references when states, Electric Distributors, or PJM develop economically differentiated 
reduction priorities in the follow-on process. Published frameworks can be inspected,

Comments of Hans Royal, Docket No. ER26-3515-000, page 5 
challenged, and updated, which is what makes them suitable as a common reference for 
operators, regulators, and lenders. 
6. Conclusion 
PJM has proposed a workable interim response to an urgent problem, and I support approval. The 
Commission should also be clear about what the interim design leaves unresolved. Large loads 
that appear similar electrically can differ by an order of magnitude in the value they lose when 
curtailed. BYONC and backup-generation choices should make part of that difference visible 
almost immediately. PJM should preserve the ability to use what it learns, instead of hardening a 
temporary pro rata approach into the long-term answer. 
Respectfully submitted, 
Hans Royal 
Author, The Compute Heat Rate (Royal, 2026)
